original.title: A scaled secant equation
original.question_html:
Use exact values throughout.

(a)[5]

Use de Moivre’s theorem to express \(\cos5\theta\) as a polynomial in \(\cos\theta\).

(b)[4]

Hence solve \(x^5+20x^4-320x^2+1024=0\), writing every root as \(2\sec(q\pi)\).

(c)[1]

Deduce the exact sum of the five secant values appearing in part (b).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Expand the fifth power and take its real part.

(b)

Use \(\cos\theta=2/x\), not \(1/x\).

(c)

Use the coefficient of \(x^4\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\) and \(u=\sin\theta\). De Moivre gives

\[(c+iu)^{5}=\cos 5\theta+i\sin 5\theta.\]

Expand and equate real parts:

\[\cos 5\theta=c^{5} - 10 c^{3} u^{2} + 5 c u^{4}.\]

Use \(u^2=1-c^2\).

\[\cos 5\theta=16 \cos^{5}\theta - 20 \cos^{3}\theta + 5 \cos\theta.\]

(b)

Put \(x=2\sec\theta\). Multiplication of \(\cos5\theta=-\tfrac12\) by \(2x^5\) produces the given polynomial.

\[5\theta=2k\pi\pm\frac{2\pi}{3}.\]

Choose \(0\leq\theta\leq\pi\), where cosine is one-to-one. The five angles are

\[\frac{2 \pi}{15},\ \frac{4 \pi}{15},\ \frac{8 \pi}{15},\ \frac{2 \pi}{3},\ \frac{14 \pi}{15}.\]

None has zero cosine. These give five distinct roots of a degree-five polynomial, so no other roots remain.

(c)

The monic polynomial has root sum \(-20\). Each polynomial root is twice its corresponding secant value.

\[\sum\sec\theta=\frac{-20}{2}=-10.\]

original.title: Four roots and principal arguments
original.question_html:
Consider \(z^{4}=-8 + 8 \sqrt{3} i\).

(a)[5]

Find all roots in exponential form, with \(-\pi\leq\arg(z)\lt\pi\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Separate modulus and argument; include all values obtained by adding multiples of \(2\pi\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

First write the right-hand side in modulus–argument form:

\[-8 + 8 \sqrt{3} i=16e^{i(\frac{2 \pi}{3})}.\]

All arguments are obtained before reducing to the requested interval:

\[\theta_k=\frac{\frac{2 \pi}{3}+2k\pi}{4},\quad k=0,\ldots,3.\]

Take the positive fourth root of the modulus. The arguments are equally spaced, so the roots are distinct.

\[z=2e^{i\theta},\qquad \theta=\frac{\pi}{6},\ \frac{2 \pi}{3},\ - \frac{5 \pi}{6},\ - \frac{\pi}{3}.\]

There are 4 distinct roots, which accounts for the degree of the equation.

original.title: A shifted sine progression
original.question_html:
Let \(n\) be a positive integer.

(a)[2]

For \(z e0\) and \(z^3 e1\), express \(\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}z^{3r+1}\) as a single quotient.

(b)[4]

Use \(z=e^{i heta}\) to obtain a product-form expression for \(\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\sin((3r+1) heta)\), when \(\sin(3 heta/2) e0\).

(c)[1]

Evaluate the sum directly when \( heta=2m\pi/3\), where \(m\) is an integer.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Identify the first term and ratio separately.

(b)

Factor out the midpoint phase before taking imaginary parts.

(c)

Do not substitute into a quotient with zero denominator.
original.solution_html:
(a)

This is a geometric progression with first term \(z\) and ratio \(z^3\), so

\[\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}z^{3r+1}=\frac{z(1-z^{3n})}{1-z^3}.\]

(b)

Use \(1-e^{iu}=-2ie^{iu/2}\sin(u/2)\). The complex sum becomes

\[e^{i(3n-1)\theta/2}\frac{\sin(3n\theta/2)}{\sin(3\theta/2)}.\]

Its imaginary part is the required sum:

\[\frac{\sin{\left(\frac{3 n \theta}{2} \right)} \sin{\left(\frac{\theta \left(3 n - 1\right)}{2} \right)}}{\sin{\left(\frac{3 \theta}{2} \right)}}\]

(c)

Each angle \((3r+1)\theta\) differs from \(\theta\) by \(2rm\pi\); all terms are equal.

original.title: A quotient of sixth powers
original.question_html:
Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), with \(\cos\theta\ne0\).

(a)[7]

By expanding \((z-z^{-1})^6\) and \((z+z^{-1})^6\), express \(\tan^6\theta\) as a quotient involving only \(\cos2\theta,\cos4\theta,\cos6\theta\) and constants.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Remember \(i^6=-1\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z-z^{-1})^{6}=z^{6} - 6 z^{4} + 15 z^{2} - 20 + \frac{15}{z^{2}} - \frac{6}{z^{4}} + \frac{1}{z^{6}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{6}i^{6}\). This gives

\[\sin^{6}\theta=- \frac{15 \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{3 \cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{16} - \frac{\cos{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{5}{16}.\]

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z+z^{-1})^{6}=z^{6} + 6 z^{4} + 15 z^{2} + 20 + \frac{15}{z^{2}} + \frac{6}{z^{4}} + \frac{1}{z^{6}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{6}i^{0}\). This gives

\[\cos^{6}\theta=\frac{15 \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{3 \cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{16} + \frac{\cos{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{5}{16}.\]

Divide the two identities. The denominator is \(32\cos^6\theta\), so the stated exclusion is exactly what is needed.

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{4}i^{4}\). This gives

original.question_html:
For integers \(n\geq0\), let \(J_n=\int_0^{\pi/3}\sin^n\theta\,d\theta\).

(a)[5]

Use de Moivre’s theorem to express \(\sin^7\theta\) as a linear combination of \(\sin\theta,\sin3\theta,\sin5\theta,\sin7\theta\).

(b)[4]

(a)

The seventh power of \(2i\sin\theta\) has a minus sign.

(b)

(c)

\[\sin^{7}\theta=\frac{35 \sin{\left(\theta \right)}}{64} - \frac{21 \sin{\left(3 \theta \right)}}{64} + \frac{7 \sin{\left(5 \theta \right)}}{64} - \frac{\sin{\left(7 \theta \right)}}{64}.\]

(b)

\[J_n=[-\sin^{n-1}\theta\cos\theta]_0^{\pi/3}+(n-1)\int_0^{\pi/3}\sin^{n-2}\theta\cos^2\theta\,d\theta.\]

The boundary term is \(-\tfrac12(\sqrt3/2)^{n-1}\). Use \(\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta\), then move \((n-1)J_n\) to the left.

\[9J_9=8J_7-\frac12\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)^8.\]

The final value is rational because the endpoint cosine values in all the odd harmonics are rational.

original.question_html:
Let \(r\gt0\), \(\theta\in\mathbb R\), and \(z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\).

(a)[4]

Prove by mathematical induction that \(z^n=r^n(\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta)\) for every positive integer \(n\).

(b)[2]

Deduce the corresponding formula for \(z^{-n}\), and explain the change in modulus and argument.
original.hint_html:
(a)

The induction step needs the addition formulae, not the conclusion you are trying to prove.

(b)

Rationalise the reciprocal using the conjugate.
original.answer_html:
(a)

The formula holds for every positive integer n.

(b)

\[z^{-n}=r^{-n}(\cos n\theta-i\sin n\theta).\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

For \(n=1\), the result is the definition of \(z\). Assume the formula holds for \(n=k\). Then

\[z^{k+1}=r^{k+1}(\cos k\theta+i\sin k\theta)(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta).\]
\[=r^{k+1}\{\cos k\theta\cos\theta-\sin k\theta\sin\theta+i(\sin k\theta\cos\theta+\cos k\theta\sin\theta)\}.\]

The addition formulae make the bracket equal to \(\cos((k+1)\theta)+i\sin((k+1)\theta)\). This proves the induction step. The result therefore holds for every positive integer.

Because \(r\gt0\), \(z^n\ne0\), and

\[\frac1{z^n}=r^{-n}\frac{\cos n\theta-i\sin n\theta}{\cos^2n\theta+\sin^2n\theta}=r^{-n}(\cos n\theta-i\sin n\theta).\]

The modulus becomes \(r^{-n}\); an argument is \(-n\theta\), reduced modulo \(2\pi\) when a principal argument is requested.

original.title: A quartic from a tangent equation
original.question_html:
All angles are in radians.

(a)[5]

Use de Moivre’s theorem to express \(\tan4\theta\) in terms of \(t=\tan\theta\).

(b)[3]

Hence solve \(\sqrt{3} t^{4} + 4 t^{3} - 6 \sqrt{3} t^{2} - 4 t + \sqrt{3}=0\), giving all four roots as tangent values.

(c)[2]

Find the exact sum of the squares of these four roots.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Take the ratio of imaginary to real parts.

(b)

Use one period of tangent to avoid repeating a root.

(c)

Use \(\sum t_j^2=(\sum t_j)^2-2\sum_{j\lt k}t_jt_k\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

For \(t=\tan\theta\), de Moivre gives

\[(1+it)^{4}=\sec^{4}\theta(\cos 4\theta+i\sin 4\theta).\]

Expanding gives the following real and imaginary parts:

\[\operatorname{Re}(1+it)^{4}=t^{4} - 6 t^{2} + 1,\qquad \operatorname{Im}(1+it)^{4}=- 4 t^{3} + 4 t.\]

Divide the imaginary part by the real part:

\[\tan 4\theta=\frac{- 4 t^{3} + 4 t}{t^{4} - 6 t^{2} + 1}.\]

This quotient requires \(\cos\theta\cos 4\theta\ne0\).

(b)

The equation gives \(\tan4\theta=\sqrt3\), so

\[4\theta=\frac\pi3+k\pi,\qquad\theta=\frac\pi{12}+\frac{k\pi}4.\]

For \(k=0,1,2,3\), the four finite tangent values are distinct. If both real and imaginary parts of \((1+it)^4\) vanished, the number itself would vanish, which is impossible for real \(t\). Thus no root is lost by division.

(c)

Divide the quartic by \(\sqrt3\). Then the root sum is \(-4/\sqrt3\), and the pairwise product sum is \(-6\).

\[\sum t_j^2=\left(-\frac4{\sqrt3}\right)^2-2(-6)=\frac{52}{3}.\]

Let \(t=\tan\theta\).

(a)[5]

(b)[2]

(b)

(c)

The sign must follow from the angle intervals.

(c)

\[\sqrt7.\]

original.question_html:

(a)[5]

Use de Moivre’s theorem to show that \(\tan5\theta=(5t-10t^3+t^5)/(1-10t^2+5t^4)\), where \(t=\tan\theta\).

(c)[4]

(a)

(c)

Expanding gives the following real and imaginary parts:

\[\operatorname{Re}(1+it)^{5}=5 t^{4} - 10 t^{2} + 1,\qquad \operatorname{Im}(1+it)^{5}=t^{5} - 10 t^{3} + 5 t.\]

Divide the imaginary part by the real part:

\[\tan 5\theta=\frac{t^{5} - 10 t^{3} + 5 t}{5 t^{4} - 10 t^{2} + 1}.\]

This quotient requires \(\cos\theta\cos 5\theta\ne0\).

\[u^{-2}-10u^{-1}+5=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad5u^2-10u+1=0.\]

\[5(v-1)^2-10(v-1)+1=5v^2-20v+16.\]

Thus \(v_1+v_2=4\) and \(v_1v_2=16/5\).

\[v_1^2+v_2^2=16-\frac{32}{5}=\frac{48}{5}.\]

original.title: Zero cotangents and a product identity
original.stem_html: Show why the discarded solution is not a root of the final quartic.
original.question_html:
Show why the discarded solution is not a root of the final quartic.

(a)[5]

Use de Moivre’s theorem to express \(\cot5\theta\) in terms of \(u=\cot\theta\).

(b)[2]

Hence find the four roots of \(u^4-10u^2+5=0\) as cotangents of rational multiples of \(\pi\).

(c)[2]

Deduce the exact value of \(\cot^2(\pi/10)\cot^2(3\pi/10)\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Take the real part over the imaginary part.

(b)

Separate the factor u before listing roots of the quartic.

(c)

Use the quadratic in the square of u.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(x=\cot\theta\). For \(\sin\theta\ne0\),

\[(x+i)^{5}=\frac{\cos 5\theta+i\sin 5\theta}{\sin^{5}\theta}.\]

The binomial expansion gives

\[\operatorname{Re}(x+i)^{5}=x^{5} - 10 x^{3} + 5 x,\qquad \operatorname{Im}(x+i)^{5}=5 x^{4} - 10 x^{2} + 1.\]

Dividing real by imaginary parts is valid when \(\sin 5\theta\ne0\):

\[\cot 5\theta=\frac{x^{5} - 10 x^{3} + 5 x}{5 x^{4} - 10 x^{2} + 1}.\]

(b)

Use \(5\theta=\pi/2+k\pi\). The five cotangents on \((0,\pi)\) include \(\cot(\pi/2)=0\). This zero comes from the separate factor \(u\) in the numerator, whereas the quartic has constant term 5. The other four values are its roots.

(c)

The squared positive cotangents solve \(v^2-10v+5=0\). Their product is therefore 5.

original.title: Cube-root algebra and a rotated square
original.question_html:
Let \(\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}\) and \(u=1-\omega\).

(a)[2]

Give \(\omega\) in Cartesian form, and show that \(1+\omega+\omega^2=0\).

(b)[4]

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\det\begin{pmatrix}1&2\omega&3\omega^2\\3\omega^2&1&2\omega\\2\omega&3\omega^2&1\end{pmatrix}\).

(c)[4]

Find all roots of \(z^4=u^4\) in exponential form, with principal arguments in \([-\pi,\pi)\).

(d)[4]

Sketch the four roots on an Argand diagram. Identify the root nearest to the point representing 2, and find the exact distance.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Factor the difference of cubes.

(b)

Use powers of omega to simplify after expanding.

(c)

Divide by u before using fourth roots of unity.

(d)

All roots have the same modulus, so nearest to 2 means largest real part.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Use the cosine and sine of \(2\pi/3\). Since \(\omega^3=1\) and \(\omega\ne1\), division of \(\omega^3-1=(\omega-1)(\omega^2+\omega+1)\) proves the sum identity.

(b)

Expand the determinant using the six signed products:

\[1+8\omega^3+27\omega^6-6\omega^3-6\omega^3-6\omega^3=1+8+27-18=18.\]

Here \(\omega^3=\omega^6=1\).

(c)

\[u=\frac32-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}i=\sqrt3e^{-i\pi/6}.\]

The equation \((z/u)^4=1\) gives \(z=u i^k\), \(k=0,1,2,3\). Add multiples of \(\pi/2\) to \(-\pi/6\), then reduce to the requested interval.

(d)

The points form a square on \(|z|=\sqrt3\), centred at the origin. For a point on this circle,

\[|z-2|^2=|z|^2+4-4\operatorname{Re}z=7-4\operatorname{Re}z.\]

The real parts of the four roots are \(3/2,\sqrt3/2,-3/2,-\sqrt3/2\). The largest is \(3/2\), belonging to \(u\). Hence the smallest squared distance is \(7-6=1\).

(a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\) and \(u=\sin\theta\). De Moivre gives

Expanding gives the following real and imaginary parts:

\[\operatorname{Re}(1+it)^{3}=1 - 3 t^{2},\qquad \operatorname{Im}(1+it)^{3}=- t^{3} + 3 t.\]

Divide the imaginary part by the real part:

original.question_html:
Let \(a\) be real. Consider \(z^4+2az^2+1=0\).

(a)[4]

Find the set of values of \(a\) for which every root has modulus 1.

(b)[3]

Within this set, determine when there are four distinct roots. Describe both endpoint cases.

(c)[4]

Find all roots when \(a=1/2\), and explain their relationship to the sixth roots of unity.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Square the roots first; use a converse as well as a construction.

(b)

Distinguish distinct values from roots counted with multiplicity.

(c)

Multiplication by z squared minus 1 introduces two values to remove.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[-1\leq a\leq1.\]

(b)

\[-1\lt a\lt1;\quad a=-1:\ z=\pm1\text{ each twice};\quad a=1:\ z=\pm i\text{ each twice}.\]

(c)

\[z=e^{ik\pi/3},\qquad k=1,2,4,5.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(w=z^2\). The two w-roots satisfy \(w^2+2aw+1=0\). If \(|a|\leq1\), they are \(-a\pm i\sqrt{1-a^2}\), both of modulus 1. Their square roots also have modulus 1.

Conversely, if all z-roots have modulus 1, so do both w-roots. Their sum is \(-2a\), so the triangle inequality gives \(2|a|\leq2\). Thus \(|a|\leq1\).

(b)

For \(-1\lt a\lt1\), the two w-roots are distinct and nonzero, and each gives two square roots; the two pairs cannot overlap. At \(a=-1\), the polynomial is \((z^2-1)^2\). At \(a=1\), it is \((z^2+1)^2\).

(c)

The equation becomes \(z^4+z^2+1=0\). Multiplication by \(z^2-1\) gives \(z^6-1=0\), but \(z=\pm1\) were introduced by that multiplication and do not satisfy the quartic. The other four sixth roots are the required roots.

original.title: Four nonzero roots from tan six theta
original.question_html:
Put \(t=\tan\theta\).

(a)[5]

Use de Moivre’s theorem to express \(\tan6\theta\) in terms of \(t\).

(b)[2]

Hence identify the four roots of \(3t^4-10t^2+3=0\) as tangent values.

(c)[2]

Find \(\sum_jt_j^2\) and \(\prod_jt_j\) for these four roots.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Expand the sixth power of 1+it.

(b)

One candidate angle has undefined tangent; another comes from the factor t.

(c)

Count each squared value twice.
original.solution_html:
(a)

For \(t=\tan\theta\), de Moivre gives

\[(1+it)^{6}=\sec^{6}\theta(\cos 6\theta+i\sin 6\theta).\]

Expanding gives the following real and imaginary parts:

\[\operatorname{Re}(1+it)^{6}=- t^{6} + 15 t^{4} - 15 t^{2} + 1,\qquad \operatorname{Im}(1+it)^{6}=6 t^{5} - 20 t^{3} + 6 t.\]

Divide the imaginary part by the real part:

\[\tan 6\theta=\frac{6 t^{5} - 20 t^{3} + 6 t}{- t^{6} + 15 t^{4} - 15 t^{2} + 1}.\]

This quotient requires \(\cos\theta\cos 6\theta\ne0\).

(b)

The numerator is \(2t(3t^4-10t^2+3)\). Set \(6\theta=k\pi\). In one tangent period, discard \(t=0\) and the undefined value at \(\theta=\pi/2\). The four remaining angles are those listed.

(c)

The two squared values solve \(3v^2-10v+3=0\), and each occurs twice among the four squared roots. Thus the square sum is \(2(10/3)=20/3\). The quartic has constant-to-leading coefficient ratio 1, so its four-root product is 1.

original.title: Two concentric root triangles
original.question_html:
Consider \(z^6-7z^3-8=0\).

(a)[3]

Factor the polynomial as a product of two cubics in \(z\).

(b)[5]

Find all six roots in exact Cartesian form.

(c)[3]

Describe the two root triangles geometrically. Find the sum of the squares of the moduli of all six roots.
original.hint_html:
(a)

First use a quadratic in z cubed.

(b)

One triangle has radius 2 and the other radius 1.

(c)

This is a sum of squared moduli, not a sum of complex squares.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[z^6-7z^3-8=(z^3-8)(z^3+1).\]

(b)

\[2,\ -1+i\sqrt3,\ -1-i\sqrt3,\ -1,\ \frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}i,\ \frac12-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}i.\]

(c)

\[\text{Equilateral triangles of radii }2\text{ and }1,\text{ rotated by }\pi/3;\qquad\sum|z_j|^2=15.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(u=z^3\). The quadratic is \(u^2-7u-8=(u-8)(u+1)\), giving the displayed factorisation.

(b)

For \(z^3=8\), the roots are \(2e^{2\pi ik/3}\). For \(z^3=-1\), the roots are \(e^{i(\pi/3+2\pi k/3)}\), \(k=0,1,2\).

Converting the six standard angles gives the stated Cartesian values. The two sets have different moduli, so they do not overlap.

(c)

Each cubic contributes three equally spaced arguments, so both triangles are equilateral with centre O. The radius-1 triangle is rotated by \(\pi/3\) relative to the radius-2 triangle.

\[\sum|z_j|^2=3\cdot2^2+3\cdot1^2=15.\]

original.stem_html: A complex-number derivation is required for the identity.
original.question_html:
A complex-number derivation is required for the identity.

(a)[4]

Use de Moivre’s theorem to express \(\cos^4u\) as a linear combination of \(1,\cos2u,\cos4u\).

(b)[3]

Hence evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/6}\cos^4(\theta+\pi/6)\,d\theta\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Expand \((z+z^{-1})^4\).

(b)

Shift both endpoints, not only the integrand.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z+z^{-1})^{4}=z^{4} + 4 z^{2} + 6 + \frac{4}{z^{2}} + \frac{1}{z^{4}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{4}i^{0}\). This gives

\[\cos^{4}\theta=\frac{\cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{2} + \frac{\cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{8} + \frac{3}{8}.\]

The identity is valid for every real angle; replace \(\theta\) by \(u\).

(b)

Put \(u=\theta+\pi/6\). Both limits move: \(u\) runs from \(\pi/6\) to \(\pi/3\).

\[\left[\frac38u+\frac14\sin2u+\frac1{32}\sin4u\right]_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3}=\frac\pi{16}-\frac{\sqrt3}{32}.\]

The sine-of-double-angle contributions cancel; the quadruple-angle contributions do not.

original.title: Six secants and an inverse-square sum
original.stem_html: Give a complete set of exact roots.
original.question_html:
Give a complete set of exact roots.

(a)[6]

Use de Moivre’s theorem to show that \(\displaystyle\sec6\theta=\frac{\sec^6\theta}{32-48\sec^2\theta+18\sec^4\theta-\sec^6\theta}\), stating the required restrictions.

(b)[4]

Hence solve \(x^{6} \left(-1 + \sqrt{2}\right) - 18 \sqrt{2} x^{4} + 48 \sqrt{2} x^{2} - 32 \sqrt{2}=0\), expressing each root as \(\sec(q\pi)\).

(c)[1]

Evaluate \(\sum_jx_j^{-2}\), where the six roots are \(x_j\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Derive the cosine identity first.

(b)

Solve the cosine equation on an interval where cosine is injective.

(c)

Use the polynomial with reversed coefficients.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\) and \(u=\sin\theta\). De Moivre gives

\[(c+iu)^{6}=\cos 6\theta+i\sin 6\theta.\]

Expand and equate real parts:

\[\cos 6\theta=c^{6} - 15 c^{4} u^{2} + 15 c^{2} u^{4} - u^{6}.\]

Use \(u^2=1-c^2\).

\[\cos 6\theta=32 \cos^{6}\theta - 48 \cos^{4}\theta + 18 \cos^{2}\theta - 1.\]

Take reciprocals, then multiply numerator and denominator by \(\sec^6\theta\). Both \(\cos\theta\) and \(\cos6\theta\) must be nonzero.

(b)

The polynomial rearranges to \(x^6=-\sqrt2(32-48x^2+18x^4-x^6)\). Thus \(\sec6\theta=-\sqrt2\), or \(\cos6\theta=-1/\sqrt2\).

\[6\theta=2k\pi\pm\frac{3\pi}{4}.\]

In \([0,\pi]\), the six angles are

\[\frac{\pi}{8},\ \frac{5 \pi}{24},\ \frac{11 \pi}{24},\ \frac{13 \pi}{24},\ \frac{19 \pi}{24},\ \frac{7 \pi}{8}.\]

None has zero cosine. The six secants are distinct and exhaust the degree of the polynomial.

(c)

The reciprocal roots are six cosines. Equivalently, the reciprocal polynomial has leading coefficient \(-32\sqrt2\), zero next coefficient, and next coefficient \(48\sqrt2\). Its pairwise-product sum is \(-3/2\), so the sum of its squared roots is \(0-2(-3/2)=3\).

(a)[6]

(a)

original.question_html:
Consider \(\left(z - 1 + 2 i\right)^{3}=- 4 \sqrt{2} + 4 \sqrt{2} i\).

There are 3 distinct roots, which accounts for the degree of the equation.

original.question_html:

(a)[6]

(b)[4]

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/3}(\cos^8(x/2)+\sin^8(x/2))\,dx\).

(c)[5]

original.hint_html:
(a)

The complementary-angle substitution saves a second full expansion.

(b)

(c)

A substitution c=cos(theta) alone would not exclude real roots outside [-1,1].

(a)

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z+z^{-1})^{8}=z^{8} + 8 z^{6} + 28 z^{4} + 56 z^{2} + 70 + \frac{56}{z^{2}} + \frac{28}{z^{4}} + \frac{8}{z^{6}} + \frac{1}{z^{8}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{8}i^{0}\). This gives

\[\cos^{8}\theta=\frac{7 \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{16} + \frac{7 \cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{\cos{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{16} + \frac{\cos{\left(8 \theta \right)}}{128} + \frac{35}{128}.\]

Apply the complementary-angle substitution to obtain the sine expression. Terms in \(\cos2\theta\) and \(\cos6\theta\) change sign, so those terms cancel on addition.

\[\frac{7 \cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{16} + \frac{\cos{\left(8 \theta \right)}}{64} + \frac{35}{64}\]

(b)

Put \(\theta=x/2\) into the identity, so the frequencies become 2 and 4 in x.

\[\left[\frac{35x}{64}+\frac7{32}\sin2x+\frac1{256}\sin4x\right]_0^{\pi/3}=\frac{35\pi}{192}+\frac{55\sqrt3}{512}.\]

original.question_html:
Do not use numerical trigonometric values.

(a)[5]

Use de Moivre’s theorem to derive \(\cos5\theta=\cos\theta(16\cos^4\theta-20\cos^2\theta+5)\).

(b)[4]

Hence find the exact values of \(\cos(\pi/10)\) and \(\cos(3\pi/10)\), justifying the choice of signs.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Take real parts of the fifth power.

(b)

Both the sign of the cosine and the order of the two squares need justification.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\) and \(u=\sin\theta\). De Moivre gives

\[(c+iu)^{5}=\cos 5\theta+i\sin 5\theta.\]

Expand and equate real parts:

\[\cos 5\theta=c^{5} - 10 c^{3} u^{2} + 5 c u^{4}.\]

Use \(u^2=1-c^2\).

\[\cos 5\theta=16 \cos^{5}\theta - 20 \cos^{3}\theta + 5 \cos\theta.\]

Factor one cosine from the polynomial.

(b)

For both angles, \(\cos5\theta=0\) but \(\cos\theta\ne0\). Therefore \(u=\cos^2\theta\) satisfies

\[16u^2-20u+5=0,\qquad u=\frac{5\pm\sqrt5}{8}.\]

original.stem_html: A product of three squares can be found without finding each square separately.
original.question_html:
A product of three squares can be found without finding each square separately.

(a)[5]

Use de Moivre’s theorem to prove \(\cos6\theta=32\cos^6\theta-48\cos^4\theta+18\cos^2\theta-1\).

(b)[4]

original.hint_html:
(a)

Eliminate sine using only even powers.

(b)

Find the polynomial for the squares, then use its coefficients.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\) and \(u=\sin\theta\). De Moivre gives

\[(c+iu)^{6}=\cos 6\theta+i\sin 6\theta.\]

Expand and equate real parts:

\[\cos 6\theta=c^{6} - 15 c^{4} u^{2} + 15 c^{2} u^{4} - u^{6}.\]

Use \(u^2=1-c^2\).

\[\cos 6\theta=32 \cos^{6}\theta - 48 \cos^{4}\theta + 18 \cos^{2}\theta - 1.\]

(b)

The three angles give \(\cos6\theta=0\). Their cosine squares are distinct and satisfy

\[32u^3-48u^2+18u-1=0.\]

They therefore exhaust the three roots. By the coefficient relations, their sum is \(48/32=3/2\) and their product is \(1/32\).

original.title: Two factors and no overlapping roots
original.question_html:
Let \(P(z)=z^7-(1+i)z^4-4z^3+4(1+i)\).

(a)[2]

Find complex constants \(a,b\) such that \(P(z)=(z^4-a)(z^3-b)\).

(b)[5]

Hence find every root in exponential form with angles in \([0,2\pi)\). Explain why there are seven distinct roots.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Compare the two middle coefficients first.

(b)

Check possible overlap by comparing moduli before comparing arguments.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[a=4,\qquad b=1+i.\]

(b)

\[z=\sqrt2e^{ik\pi/2},\ k=0,1,2,3;\qquad z=2^{1/6}e^{i(\pi/12+2k\pi/3)},\ k=0,1,2.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Expansion gives \(z^7-bz^4-az^3+ab\). Compare the coefficients of \(z^4\) and \(z^3\); the constant term then also agrees.

(b)

The first factor gives \(z^4=4\): radius \(4^{1/4}=\sqrt2\), with four arguments separated by \(\pi/2\). The second gives \(z^3=1+i=\sqrt2e^{i\pi/4}\): radius \(2^{1/6}\), with arguments \(\pi/12,3\pi/4,17\pi/12\).

The families have different moduli, \(\sqrt2\ne2^{1/6}\), so no root occurs in both. All seven are distinct.

original.title: A rotated pentagon and its nearest vertex
original.question_html:
Let \(w\) be any root of \(z^5=16+16\sqrt3i\).

(a)[1]

Write down the fifth roots of unity.

(b)[4]

Find the five roots of the given equation in exponential form and sketch them on an Argand diagram.

(c)[3]

Express \(\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^4(w/2)^j\) as a quotient in terms of \(w\).

(d)[3]

Identify the root nearest to the point representing 3, and give the exact minimum distance.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use a complete turn divided into five equal angles.

(b)

Rotate the fifth roots of unity, then scale by 2.

(c)

Use the known fifth power of w/2.

(d)

For fixed radius, nearest to a positive real point means largest cosine.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[e^{2k\pi i/5},\quad k=0,1,2,3,4.\]

(b)

\[z_k=2e^{i(\pi/15+2k\pi/5)},\quad k=0,1,2,3,4.\]

(c)

\[\frac{1-i\sqrt3}{2-w}.\]

(d)

\[z=2e^{i\pi/15},\qquad d_{\min}=\sqrt{13-12\cos(\pi/15)}.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

They have unit modulus and arguments separated by \(2\pi/5\).

(b)

\[16+16\sqrt3i=32e^{i\pi/3}.\]

Take fifth roots: the radius is 2 and the initial angle is \(\pi/15\). Multiplication by the fifth roots of unity generates the other four roots. The sketch is a regular pentagon centred at the origin, rotated by \(\pi/15\).

(c)

Since \((w/2)^5=(1+i\sqrt3)/2\ne1\), in particular \(w\ne2\). Apply the geometric formula:

\[\sum_{j=0}^4(w/2)^j=\frac{1-(w/2)^5}{1-w/2}=\frac{(1-i\sqrt3)/2}{(2-w)/2}=\frac{1-i\sqrt3}{2-w}.\]

(d)

(d)[4]

(b)

(c)

(d)

original.answer_html:
(a)

\[\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\cos(r\delta)=\frac{\sin(n\delta/2)\cos((n-1)\delta/2)}{\sin(\delta/2)}.\]

(b)

\[\int_0^{\pi/6}\cos2x\,dx\lt U_n=\frac{\pi}{12n}\frac{\cos(\pi/6-\pi/(6n))}{\sin(\pi/(6n))}.\]

(c)

(a)

\[\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}e^{ir\delta}=\frac{1-e^{in\delta}}{1-e^{i\delta}}=e^{i(n-1)\delta/2}\frac{\sin(n\delta/2)}{\sin(\delta/2)}.\]

To obtain the second equality, factor \(-2i e^{in\delta/2}\) from the numerator and \(-2i e^{i\delta/2}\) from the denominator. The remaining sine quotient is real. Equating real parts proves the formula.

(b)

The width is \(h=\pi/(6n)\). The function is strictly decreasing on the interval, so the left-endpoint rectangles lie above it except at their left edges.

(c)

Right endpoints give

The two sums share all interior endpoint terms. Thus

\[U_n-L_n=\frac{\pi}{6n}\left(1-\cos\frac\pi3\right)=\frac{\pi}{12n}.\]

Subtract this gap from the expression in (b) to obtain the stated lower bound.

(d)

\[\int_0^{\pi/6}\cos2x\,dx=\left[\frac12\sin2x\right]_0^{\pi/6}=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}.\]

The integral is between the bounds, whose gap tends to zero; hence both bounds tend to the integral.

\[\frac{\pi}{12n}\lt\frac{\pi}{12000}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\gt1000.\]

The value 1000 gives equality, not the required strict inequality. The least admissible integer is therefore 1001.

(a)

\[\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}w^k=\frac{1-w^n}{1-w}.\]

original.question_html:
Let \(n\) be a positive integer.

(a)[2]

If \(w^n=1\) and \(w\ne1\), prove that \(1+w+\cdots+w^{n-1}=0\).

(b)[6]

By considering powers of \(z=\tfrac25e^{i\theta}\), find closed forms for \(\displaystyle C=\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}(2/5)^r\cos r\theta\) and \(\displaystyle S=\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}(2/5)^r\sin r\theta\). Justify convergence.

(c)[2]

(b)

The series starts at r=1, so its numerator is z, not 1.

(c)

(a)

The sum is \((1-w^n)/(1-w)\). Its numerator is zero and its denominator is not, so the sum is zero. The restriction \(w\ne1\) is essential: when \(w=1\), the sum is \(n\).

(b)

Since \(|z|=2/5\lt1\), the complex geometric series converges absolutely. Both real and imaginary series also converge absolutely by comparison with \(\sum(2/5)^r\).

\[C+iS=\frac{z}{1-z}=\frac{z(1-\overline z)}{|1-z|^2}=\frac{(2/5)(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)-4/25}{29/25-(4/5)\cos\theta}.\]

Multiply numerator and denominator by 25 and equate real and imaginary parts. The denominator is at least \(29-20=9\), so the formulae are valid for every real \(\theta\).

(c)

Substitute \(\cos(\pi/3)=1/2\) and \(\sin(\pi/3)=\sqrt3/2\). The common denominator is 19, and the two numerators are 1 and \(5\sqrt3\).

original.title: Differentiating an even-multiple sine sum
original.question_html:
Let \(n\geq2\) be an integer.

(a)[6]

By considering \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}z^{2r}\), where \(z=e^{i\theta}\), prove that \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\sin2r\theta=\frac{\sin n\theta\sin((n+1)\theta)}{\sin\theta}\), for \(\sin\theta\ne0\).

(b)[5]

Hence show that \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}2r\cos(r\pi/n)=-n-\operatorname{cosec}^{2}(\pi/(2n))\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

The phase after cancellation is (n+1)theta, not ntheta.

(b)

Keep n constant during differentiation; substitute the angle at the end.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}z^{2r}=z^2\frac{1-z^{2n}}{1-z^2}.\]

Substitute \(z=e^{i\theta}\) and factor numerator and denominator about their half angles:

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}e^{2ri\theta}=e^{i(n+1)\theta}\frac{\sin n\theta}{\sin\theta}.\]

The sine quotient is real, so the imaginary part gives the required sum. Division is valid precisely under the stated restriction.

(b)

This is a finite sum, so differentiate term by term. Put \(\alpha=\pi/(2n)\) only after differentiating. For \(A(\theta)=\sin n\theta\sin((n+1)\theta)\),

\[A(\alpha)=\cos\alpha,\qquad A\prime(\alpha)=-(n+1)\sin\alpha.\]

The quotient rule therefore gives

\[\left.\frac d{d\theta}\frac{A(\theta)}{\sin\theta}\right|_{\theta=\alpha}=-(n+1)-\cot^2\alpha=-n-\operatorname{cosec}^2\alpha.\]

The differentiated left side is \(\sum 2r\cos(2r\alpha)=\sum 2r\cos(r\pi/n)\), as required.

Let \(n\geq2\) be an integer.

(a)[5]

Use a complex geometric series to prove \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\cos2r\theta=\frac{\sin n\theta\cos((n+1)\theta)}{\sin\theta}\), for \(\sin\theta\ne0\).

original.hint_html:
(a)

Use both the first term and the common ratio in the geometric series.

(b)

The derivative of a cosine contributes a minus sign.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}e^{2ri\theta}=e^{2i\theta}\frac{1-e^{2ni\theta}}{1-e^{2i\theta}}=e^{i(n+1)\theta}\frac{\sin n\theta}{\sin\theta}.\]

Take real parts. The quotient is real and defined under the stated restriction, so this yields the identity.

The quotient derivative at \(\alpha\) is

\[\frac{n\cos\alpha\sin\alpha+\sin\alpha\cos\alpha}{\sin^2\alpha}=(n+1)\cot\alpha.\]

The derivative of the left side is \(-\sum2r\sin2r\theta\). Move the minus sign to obtain the required result.

original.title: A binomial sum with weights
original.question_html:
Let \(n\geq1\) be an integer and \(0\lt\theta\lt\pi\).

(a)[2]

Prove that \(r\binom nr=n\binom{n-1}{r-1}\) for \(1\leq r\leq n\).

(b)[5]

By considering \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{n}r\binom nr z^r\), with \(z=e^{i\theta}\), find closed forms for the corresponding cosine and sine sums.

(c)[2]

Evaluate both sums in (b) when \(n=5\) and \(\theta=\pi/3\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Cancel r from r factorial.

(b)

Shift the index after using the identity in part (a).

(c)

Calculate the amplitude and phase separately.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[r\binom nr=n\binom{n-1}{r-1}.\]

(b)

\[\begin{aligned}\sum_{r=0}^{n}r\binom nr\cos r\theta&=n2^{n-1}\cos^{n-1}(\theta/2)\cos((n+1)\theta/2),\\\sum_{r=0}^{n}r\binom nr\sin r\theta&=n2^{n-1}\cos^{n-1}(\theta/2)\sin((n+1)\theta/2).\end{aligned}\]

(c)

\[\text{Cosine sum}=-45,\qquad\text{sine sum}=0.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[r\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}=\frac{n!}{(r-1)!(n-r)!}=n\frac{(n-1)!}{(r-1)!(n-r)!}.\]

The factorials are defined under the given index restriction.

(b)

The term for \(r=0\) vanishes. Apply (a), then put \(j=r-1\):

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}r\binom nr z^r=nz\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{j}z^j=nz(1+z)^{n-1}.\]

Use \(1+e^{i\theta}=2\cos(\theta/2)e^{i\theta/2}\). De Moivre gives

\[nz(1+z)^{n-1}=n2^{n-1}\cos^{n-1}(\theta/2)e^{i(n+1)\theta/2}.\]

Equate real and imaginary parts to obtain the two formulae.

(c)

The amplitude is \(5\cdot2^4(\sqrt3/2)^4=45\). The phase is \((5+1)\pi/6=\pi\), so its cosine is \(-1\) and its sine is 0.
